Contribute with translational research to a better understanding of one of the most aggressive forms of cancer. The PhD candidate pancreatic cancer at the LUMC investigates how tumour characteristics, body composition and treatment outcomes are interrelated. You will work with unique patient cohorts and advanced techniques, from transcriptomics to AI-driven analyses. Collaboration with researchers from the Netherlands and abroad offers plenty of scope to develop scientific expertise and present results internationally.
What are you gonna do?
The PhD research focuses on the relationship between body composition, treatment response and survival in patients with pancreatic cancer(PDAC). In doing so, you will investigate which tumour characteristics are associated with changes in body composition and clinical outcomes. For this, you combine clinical data and patient material with transcriptomics, imaging mass cytometry and CT-based analyses. The aim is to identify tumour-related factors that may provide new targets for future treatments.
Your main tasks are:
Collection and processing of clinical data, imaging data and patient material from various Dutch medical centers.
Performing omics analyses, spatial imaging and statistical and bioinformatical analyses.
Establishment and coordination of a translational research infrastructure
Developing new prognostic models.
Writing scientific publications and presenting research results at national and international conferences.
The findings can be validated with prospectively collected biomaterials and extensively characterized patient cohorts within the international ONCOVERS consortium.
Where are you going to work?
The Research Laboratory of the department of Stomach, Darm and Liver Diseases is the home of this PhD research. From the LUMC you work intensively with researchers from Amsterdam UMC and Maastricht UMC+. The research is embedded in ONCoverse, a large international research consortium that wants to better understand the biological complexity of pancreatic cancer and improve patient treatment.
An important basis for the research is the national biobank infrastructure for pancreatic cancer. This contains material from over 3,000 patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), collected within the Pearl SNOER initiative. The combination of these patient cohorts, prospectively collected biomaterials and collaboration between different research centres offers a strong translational research environment.
Cooperation is central to the project. Researchers, analysts and surgeons from different centres bring together their expertise and there are contacts with researchers at home and abroad. The counseling is with Dr. Luuk Hawinkels (LUMC), prof. Dr. Maarten Bijlsma (Amsterdam UMC), dr. Sander Rensen and Prof. Dr. Steven Olde Damink (Maastricht UMC+).
What are you taking?
Curiosity about translational research and the motivation to acquire new techniques and knowledge are important. In a multidisciplinary team you work effectively together, while conducting independent research is also going well. In doing so, organise and coordinate your work carefully and take your initiative to further the research.
In addition, you have:
A completed or almost completed master's programme in Biomedical Sciences, Biopharmaceutical Sciences, Medical Biology, Medicine, Life Sciences or a related programme.
Shows a visible interest in oncology, metabolism and bioinformatics and affinity with clinical and translational research.
Excellent oral and written command of English; The Dutch is a pré.
Ready to work regularly with and travel to partner institutes, including Amsterdam UMC and Maastricht UMC+.
What are we offering you?
Health driven; That's our mission. This is of course true not only for our patients but also for our employees. We aim to create a safe, inclusive and equal working environment in which talent development and connecting leadership are central. In order to continue to learn and develop, we offer internal training and further training. In addition, you are entitled to an end-of-year allowance (8.3%), holiday allowance, cycling scheme, sports budget, homework allowance and an excellent travel allowance for commuting. You are also a member of the ABP pension fund as a member of the LUMC. This means that as much as 70% of your pension contribution is paid by the LUMC and therefore you have a net increase in salary. It's so nice!

As an academic medical centre, the LUMC aims to create a staff file that reflects society. As a PhD student, you will investigate how we can better predict, diagnose and treat heart failure in children with hereditary heart muscle diseases. You focus on dilatating cardiomyopathy (DCM), a rare but severe cardiac muscle disease that can lead to heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias and premature death. Although treatment is currently largely symptomatic, new, more targeted therapies are being developed internationally. To enable these developments, a thorough understanding of the disease, genetic causes and factors affecting the quality of life is needed.
The research is part of the national PRECISE consortium and is carried out in close collaboration with patient organisations and a wide network of doctors and researchers from other UMCs in the Netherlands.

You will contribute to a rural infrastructure for research into DCM at child age by integrating clinical, genetic and imaging data into a national database.
You will investigate which early characteristics predict which children develop a more serious course, with special attention to genetic factors, echocardiographic and other imaging parameters, and additional disorders.
You study the yield and clinical impact of modern genetic diagnostics, including short-read and long-read whole genome sequencing, in patients where no genetic cause could be identified until now.
You evaluate the diagnosis and treatment of children with a suspicion of myocardiitis, with the aim of developing nationwide diagnostic and treatment protocols.
You will explore with patients and parents which factors affect the quality of life of children and young adults with DCM, so that we can improve patient guidance focused in the coming years.
You will also translate research results into scientific publications and present them at national and international conferences. This not only builds new knowledge, but also a valuable scientific network.

Tuberculosis has a mysterious protein secretion system, ESX-4, which can be lethal to the bacteria itself in activation. We're going to unravel how ESX-4 is regulated, with the aim of discovering a way to let the bacteria shut itself down. Mycobacterium tuberculosis has an impenetrable cell wall. To functionalize this cell wall, the bacteria has five different protein secretion systems, also called ESX systems. Some of these systems are essential for the growth or virulence of the bacteria. However, we know little about ESX-4. Recently, we have discovered that the production of this system is precisely regulated by the peptide WerA and the regulator WerB. Disabling these proteins leads to strong activation of ESX-4 and the production of various possible toxins. This activation is harmful to the bacteria itself. In this project you will investigate the function of these possible toxins. In addition, you unravel which signal and which mechanism are responsible for the induction of ESX-4. Eventually, we want to disrupt this system, which may cause tuberculosis to poison itself. We conduct this research in collaboration with Radboud University, where a PhD candidate for this project is also appointed. The project is funded by NWO. You will conduct laboratory research into the functioning and regulation of the ESX-4 system in pathogenic mycobacteria. Your work will include: Experimenting with bacterial cultures. Performing genetic and molecular analyses. Working with microscopy. Analyzing data, including proteomics and transcriptomics data. Studying proteins, including possible toxins. Many experiments are carried out with the model organism Mycobacterium marinum. You also investigate the tuberculosis bacteria itself, a BSL-3 organism. For this PhD position we're looking for a researcher with a

strong interest in microbiological and biomolecular research. You also bring the following: A completed master's programme in microbiology, biomedical or biomolecular sciences, biochemistry or a similar direction. Experience with molecular-biological and microbiological techniques, such as genetic engineering, protein and DNA/RNA analysis and working with bacterial cultures. An analytical and independent work capability. You can systematically examine complex biological issues and interpret research results critically. Good communication and cooperation skills. Strong motivation for scientific research and the willingness to learn new techniques and skills. Experience with M. tuberculosis or work under BSL-3 conditions is not required. Central Holland is located in the heart of the Randstad. The municipalities of Bodegraven-Reeuwijk, Gouda, Krimpenerwaard, Waddinxveen and Zuidplas are working together on a structural basis, from one course, on a vital region where it is well-living, working and entrepreneurship.

Working together. You connect the right people in the right setting and are a real team player in it.

More at National Water and Soil Traineeship
Are you a newly graduated Hbo or wo-worf with passion for the rural area? Are you ready to make a meaningful contribution to the great transition challenges of this time? Then the National Traineeship Rural Area (NTLG) is exactly what you're looking for!
About the traineeship
With the NTLG we offer you a flying start in the field of rural areas: the place where large transitions around nitrogen, biodiversity, nature and climate come together. An effective approach to these transitions requires a new generation of professionals with a fresh and broad look . You can be this! Essentially, you learn to look beyond the boundaries of your own organization and assignment. That is why our two-year trainee program offers space for both substantive and personal development, which benefits both you and the trainee and the organisation you work on.
You will get started with various themes such as the transition of agriculture, broad prosperity and spatial planning, and will have the opportunity to visit various organisations together with your fellow trainees and build a valuable network. In addition, you will participate with your trainee group in a reality game that you will play for two years and in which you will work on challenging issues in an interactive and effective way.
This is what you're going to do as a trainee area development . .
If you walk, cycle, sail or drive in the rural area of Drenthe and Groningen, you will soon find Prolander. Prolander's main task is to realize the Netherlands Nature Network. This network strengthens and connects important nature reserves. Together with regional partners, Prolander is looking for solutions that contribute to strong nature and perspective for agriculture. There is also attention to water storage and recreation. Prolander is working on a major social issue: How do we ensure a sustainable future for the rural area?
To make that future possible, much must be done behind the scenes. Think of acquiring land, advising on subsidies, creating spatial designs, jointly drawing up layout plans and the actual layout of an area. At Prolander you work with more than 150 colleagues on the whole process: from design to realization.
One of these challenges is the programme Growing Coast . Within this programme, Prolander is responsible for the elaboration and implementation of Pillar 1: raising agricultural land with sludge from the Ems-Dollard. The project has a long run, but is still at the beginning of its implementation. There is therefore plenty of room to think with and shape the approach. For this project we are looking for a trainee who likes to pioneer, take initiative and like to switch between different interests and organisations.
Project objective
